case_analysis.focal_point: Whether lower federal courts may entertain a constitutional challenge (facial or as-applied) to FECA’s limits on coordinated political party expenditures when the Supreme Court in Colorado II upheld those limits against a materially identical facial First Amendment challenge, absent an unmistakable signal that intervening Supreme Court doctrine has displaced Colorado II.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Election Campaign Act (FECA) coordinated party expenditure limits (as upheld in FEC v. Colorado Republican Federal Campaign Committee (Colorado II)), challenged under the First Amendment (speech and association).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Plaintiffs (petitioners) argue that FECA’s coordinated party expenditure limits violate the First Amendment because coordinated party spending should be treated like protected political expression/association rather than as regulable contributions; they contend Colorado II should not control because subsequent doctrinal developments in campaign-finance law have undermined its reasoning and because they present additional or refined arguments and evidence not previously considered, attempting to proceed at least as an as-applied challenge even if a facial challenge is foreclosed.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The FEC (respondent) argues the challenge is foreclosed by Colorado II, which expressly rejected the core claim that all coordinated party expenditure limits are unconstitutional; lower courts are bound to follow directly applicable Supreme Court precedent even if later cases cast doubt on its reasoning, and any effort to relitigate the same factual and legal basis through an as-applied label is an impermissible end-run around stare decisis (with any overruling reserved to the Supreme Court).

Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Kennedy v. Bremerton clarifies the only conceivable off-ramp—“long ago abandoned” doctrine—but that exception is narrow and, as Justice Kagan notes, none of our later decisions squarely repudiates Colorado II’s holding on coordinated party expenditures or makes it irreconcilable to apply. Justice Barrett is also right that styling the challenge as “as-applied” cannot avoid directly controlling precedent when the requested rule would invalidate the very limits Colorado II upheld in their ordinary operation. Given reliance interests and the need for stable election rules, any reconsideration of Colorado II should be reserved for a case where we take that question head-on rather than inviting anticipatory overruling by inferior courts.

case_analysis.respondent_position: The FEC (respondent) argues that Colorado II directly controls because it expressly rejected essentially the same constitutional claim (that coordinated party expenditure limits are unconstitutional), that lower courts are bound to follow Supreme Court precedent under Rodriguez de Quijas even if later cases cast doubt on the reasoning, and that plaintiffs cannot evade Colorado II by repackaging the same factual and legal theory as an as-applied challenge or by urging a lower court to anticipate overruling.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s originalist critique is the strongest push, but it is fundamentally an invitation for us to overrule Colorado II, which squarely upheld these coordinated party-expenditure limits as contribution-like on anticircumvention grounds. As Justice Alito and Justice Barrett emphasize, nothing since has “entirely displaced” that specific holding, and under Rodriguez de Quijas lower courts properly treated it as controlling rather than anticipating our reversal based on doctrinal drift. Petitioners’ “as-applied” framing does not materially alter the operative burden—§ 30116(d)’s cap on coordinated spending—so the narrow, institutionally cautious course is to affirm under Colorado II and leave any reconsideration for a case that cleanly presents stare decisis factors and the full overruling question. That approach resolves no more than necessary while preserving stability in election-law rules where reliance and administrability interests are substantial.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito are right that Rodriguez de Quijas binds lower courts to follow Colorado II, but that principle has no force against this Court’s own duty to correct constitutional error; institutional minimalism cannot justify continuing an atextual limitation on core political speech. Colorado II’s “coordinated equals contribution-like” reclassification rests on anti-circumvention theories untethered to the Constitution’s original understanding of “corruption” as quid pro quo bribery, so it permits Congress to impose what functionally operates as an expenditure limit on party advocacy. Justice Sotomayor’s emphasis on “appearance” and conduit risks likewise cannot expand the government’s interest beyond actual quid pro quo corruption without diluting the First Amendment’s original public meaning. Because the statutory cap burdens protected party-candidate advocacy and cannot be justified by a historically grounded corruption interest, I would overrule Colorado II to the extent it sustains these limits and vote for petitioner.

As the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, Colorado II expressly treated coordinated party spending as contribution-like and upheld these limits on anticircumvention/corruption-prevention grounds; petitioners’ “as-applied” label does not introduce facts that take the case outside that rule. Nor do later cases “entirely displace” Colorado II in the narrow Kennedy v. Bremerton sense Justice Gorsuch notes—tension is not abandonment—so administrability and stability counsel adherence absent a case squarely presenting stare decisis factors for overruling. Given the practical consequence that parties can serve as conduits for evasion of candidate limits, the statute still fits on the contribution side of Buckley under our existing framework.

As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Colorado II directly upheld these coordinated-expenditure caps on an anticircumvention theory, and Rodriguez de Quijas underscores that perceived doctrinal drift in later cases cannot license treating a still-controlling holding as defunct. Pragmatically, eliminating these caps would predictably increase large-donor leverage through party committees and undermine equal access and confidence in democratic participation—harms Congress targeted and Colorado II recognized as contribution-like risks.

Petitioners’ effort to reframe the challenge as “as-applied” or premised on intervening doctrine does not materially alter the legal theory Colorado II resolved, and Kennedy v. Bremerton does not license inferior courts to treat a still-binding decision as displaced absent a clear abandonment by this Court. Accordingly, the coordinated-expenditure limits remain constitutional under existing precedent, and lower courts may not revisit the question on the premise of doctrinal erosion.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Colorado II, 533 U.S. 431 (2001), directly upheld FECA’s coordinated national party expenditure limits by treating them as contribution limits justified by anti-circumvention and corruption-prevention interests, and the petitioners’ reframed challenge would effectively negate that holding. Under Rodriguez de Quijas v. Shearson/Am. Exp., Inc., 490 U.S. 477, 484 (1989), lower courts must follow controlling Supreme Court precedent even if later doctrine arguably undermines its reasoning, leaving reconsideration to this Court. As a matter of procedural fairness and administrability, allowing lower courts to “revisit” Colorado II based on perceived doctrinal drift would destabilize election-law rules and invite inconsistent results across jurisdictions. On this record, the proper disposition is to apply Colorado II and sustain FECA’s coordinated-expenditure limits unless and until this Court expressly overrules them.
